title: Khatm: the whole book
hook: finishing a whole reading, often in Ramadan, with a gathering

segments.voice: Yesterday, handling the mushaf: purity to touch it, a high place, never the trash. Your line was keep it high. What did you give a better place? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

It's late on one of the last nights of Ramadan. The mosque is fuller than it's been all month. Children are awake long past their bedtimes. The imam is reciting An-Nas, the very last surah, and in many mosques, when he finishes, he goes straight back to the beginning and recites the opening of the book again. Then comes a long supplication. Some people are weeping; others are already handing out sweets. The whole book, finished. Today: khatm.
screen: `A LATE NIGHT IN RAMADAN.` → `THE LAST SURAH, THEN THE FIRST.` → `WEEPING, AND SWEETS.`

segments.voice: Khatm means a seal, a finishing. It's the same root as khatam, the seal, in the title Muslims give the Prophet ﷺ: the seal of the prophets. For the Qur'an, a khatm is one complete reading, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas. Ramadan is its season. The hadith collections say the angel Jibril went over the whole Qur'an with the Prophet every Ramadan, and twice in the year he died. So many Muslims try to finish at least one full reading during the month, alone at home, or by hearing it across the nights of tarawih, one juz' a night. When a mosque reaches the end, it's often a gathering, with a special supplication after the last surah, the du'a of khatm, often long and often tearful. There's a report that the companion Anas ibn Malik, when he finished the Qur'an, would gather his family and make du'a with them. Customs vary widely. In some places a child's first khatm is celebrated with a party and new clothes: in parts of South Asia it's called an Ameen, in Turkey a hatim. And in many places the reader who finishes An-Nas begins again at once from al-Fatiha, so the reading never really stops. How often? You met one hadith in the week of the thirty parts: once a month, and not faster than seven days. Another says the one who finishes in less than three days hasn't understood it. So speed isn't the point. Many people take a year, or several. A page a day finishes a standard mushaf in under two years. The point is the whole: not only the parts you love, but every page, once.
screen: `KHATM: A SEAL, A FINISHING` · `RAMADAN IS ITS SEASON` · `A GATHERING, A SUPPLICATION` · `BEGIN AGAIN FROM AL-FATIHA`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan next year's reading. Sit, and ask what's true for you. A juz' a day, a page a day, a few verses a day, or listening to one reciter through the whole book. There are about six hundred pages in a standard mushaf. Pick an amount you could keep on a bad day, not only a good one. If you're here to learn about the path rather than practice it, choose a translation of the meanings and a pace. Hold the plan quietly. The bell holds the time.
Khatm. A seal: one complete reading of the Qur'an, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas, often finished in Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: the whole book, once. Today, write your plan somewhere you'll see it: how much, when in the day, and the date you hope to finish. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Muslims complete a full reading of the Qur'an in Ramadan, at home or through the tarawih prayers, and mosques and families often mark a khatm with a gathering, a special supplication and food.

original.note: Arabic: a seal, a completion; a full reading of the Qur'an. same root as khatam, seal.

trapdoor: what you thought: finishing a book.
what it means: a seal: one complete reading, often marked with a gathering and a supplication.
what a scholar hears: the root of khatam, seal, and the old custom of the one who arrives and sets out again, beginning anew from the Fatiha.
